prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Tonight I light the candles of my eyes in the lee And swing down this branch full of red leaves. Yellow moon, skull and spine of the hare, Arrow me to town on the neck of the air. I hear the undertaker make love in the heather; The candy maker, poor fellow, is under the weather. Skunk, moose, raccoon, they go to the doors in threes With a torch in their hands or pleas: "O, please . . ." Baruch Spinoza and the butcher are drunk: One is the tail and one is the trunk Of a beast who dances in circles for beer And doesn't think twice to learn how to steer. Our clock is blind, our clock is dumb. Its hands are broken, its fingers numb. No time for the martyr of our fair town Who wasn't a witch because she could drown. Now the dogs of the cemetery are starting to bark At the vision of her, bobbing up through the dark. When she opens her mouth to gasp for air, A moth flies out and lands in her hair. The apples are thumping, winter is coming. The lips of the pumpkin soon will be humming. By the caw of the crow on the first of the year, Something will die, something appear.

Here are two polished versions of your text. Depending on your preferred style, you can choose between **Refined Poetic Verse** (which enhances the original rhyming rhythm and meter) or **Literary Gothic Prose** (which presents the narrative as sophisticated, atmospheric prose).

---

### Option 1: Refined Poetic Verse (Maintains rhyme & rhythm)

Tonight, within the sheltered lee, I light the candles of my gaze,  
And swing down from a bough ablaze with crimson leaves.  
Beneath a yellow moon, past the hare’s pale skull and spine,  
I am arrowed to the town upon the neck of the midnight wind.  

I hear the mortician making love amidst the wild heather,  
While the poor candy maker languishes, unwell beneath the weather.  
Skunk, moose, and raccoon advance to the doors in threes,  
Bearing aloft flaming torches or softly whispered pleas: *"O, please . . ."*  

Baruch Spinoza and the butcher are blind with drink,  
Joined as the trunk and tail of a beast upon the brink—  
A creature dancing in circles, bribed only by beer,  
Heedless of direction, caring nothing to steer.  

Our clock stands blind; our clock stands mute.  
Its hands are shattered, its fingers frozen and destitute.  
It keeps no time for the gentle martyr of our fair town,  
Deemed no witch only because she was left to drown.  

Now, the cemetery hounds begin their frantic bark  
At the apparition of her form, bobbing upward through the dark.  
And as she parts her lips to gasp for long-lost air,  
A pale moth escapes, alighting gently in her hair.  

The fallen apples thump; winter draws near.  
Soon, the carved pumpkin’s lips will hum for all to hear.  
By the crow’s stark call when the new year draws algorithmically night,  
Something must perish, and something come to light.

---

### Option 2: Literary Gothic Prose (Elevated story format)

Tonight, sheltered in the lee, I light the candles of my eyes and swing down from a branch heavy with crimson leaves. Beneath an amber moon, guided by the bleached skull and spine of the hare, I am shot like an arrow toward the town upon the crest of the wind. 

In the wild heather, I overhear the undertaker indulging in love, while the poor confectioner lies stricken and unwell. Skunk, moose, and raccoon approach the doorsteps in triads, bearing aloft flaming torches or murmuring desperate pleas: *"O, please . . ."*

Baruch Spinoza and the village butcher stumble in a drunken stupor, forming the front and hind quarters of a festive beast that spins aimlessly for beer, utterly unconcerned with steering its course. Meanwhile, our town clock remains blind and mute, its hands shattered and its fingers numb. It keeps no time for our fair town’s martyr—proven innocent of witchcraft only because she drowned.

Now, the cemetery dogs begin to bark at her ghost, bobbing upward through the gloom. As she opens her mouth to gasp for air, a moth flutters forth and nestles in her hair. Fallen apples thump against the cooling earth, heralding winter's arrival; soon, the glowing pumpkin's lips will begin to hum. By the crow's stark caw on the first day of the year, one thing shall perish, and another shall appear.

Here is a complete prose rewrite of the poem, keeping all original details and facts while using entirely different phrasing and sentence structures:

***

On a sheltered evening, my gaze brightens as I leap down from a tree limb covered in red autumn leaves. Guided by the pale golden moonlight and the skeletal remains of a rabbit, the wind carries me rapidly toward the village like a shot arrow. 

As I arrive, I hear the mortician sharing romantic intimacy among the wild heather plants, while the town's confectioner lies sick in bed. Nearby, a trio of animals—a skunk, a moose, and a raccoon—visit residential doorways holding flaming torches or making earnest pleas. 

Meanwhile, the philosopher Baruch Spinoza and the local meat-cutter have become heavily intoxicated. Together, they form the front and back ends of a costumed beast that twirls wildly in search of alcohol, completely unconcerned with controlling its direction. 

The village timepiece is entirely nonfunctional and silent; its sight is gone, and its broken hands have lost all sensation and movement. No one has time to remember the town’s female martyr, whose death by drowning paradoxically proved she was innocent of sorcery. Now, the graveyard hounds begin to bark as her spirit drifts upward through the shadows. The moment her phantom jaws part to draw breath, a moth exits her throat and settles on her hair. 

Fruit thuds against the ground as the cold season approaches, and carved gourds will soon begin to produce humming sounds. Ultimately, when a black bird calls out on the first day of the new year, one life will end just as another emerges.
outputs.L3:
As the last embers of twilight faded, I set out on a journey into the heart of the valley, drawn forward by the unsettling pull of the autumn night. The air tasted of woodsmoke and damp earth, crisp with the scent of turn and decay. Above the gnarled canopy of bare trees hung a heavy, sickly yellow moon—a bloated lantern casting long, distorted shadows across the winding path. Every rustle of dry leaves sounded like a whispered warning, yet the pale amber glow illuminated my way, beckoning me toward the glow of the distant town.

Upon entering the settlement, the quiet night shattered into a fever dream of chaotic revelry. The boundaries between the living, the grotesque, and the forgotten had worn thin. Eccentric townspeople, clad in tattered rags and velvet cloaks, mingled with strange creatures masked in bone and burlap. They swarmed the cobblestone streets in a frenzy of nocturnal rituals. Door-to-door trick-or-treating was rendered uncanny—a shadowy dance where knocking on heavy wooden doors felt less like a game and more like an incantation, demanding tribute to appease whatever lurked in the dark corners of the night.

Suddenly, the manic energy of the streets collapsed into a heavy, suffocating silence. The hands of the central clock tower shuddered and froze; time itself seemed to fracture and break across the town. From the wrought-iron gates of the local cemetery, a thick, freezing mist rolled outward, carrying with it a profound sense of sorrow. Out of the fog emerged the ghostly vision of a drowned martyr, weeping luminescent water that dripped onto the dry earth. The apparition floated inches above the ground, a sorrowful reminder of past tragedies, holding the frozen town in a spell of quiet horror before dissolving back into the stones.

No sooner had the phantom vanished than the atmosphere shifted abruptly, shaken by a violent seasonal turn. The lingering warmth of the autumn fires was violently snuffed out as winter arrived not with a gentle snowfall, but with a heavy, thumping urgency. A bitter wind slammed through the alleys like a physical weight, cracking windows and coating the cobblestones in a sudden layer of black ice. Frost crept up the walls of the houses in razor-sharp patterns, and the sudden, heavy pulse of the deep freeze rattled the very foundations of the valley.

Yet, within this sudden cold lay the quiet rhythm of an ancient balance. As the calendar turned toward the new year, the oppressive darkness revealed its true purpose. This was not merely an ending, but a necessary, mystical cycle—a grand cosmic ritual of death and renewal. In the frozen silence, under the quiet blanket of snow, the old world surrendered its life so that something new could spark beneath the soil. The night reminded all who witnessed it that decay is simply the soil for rebirth, and that darkness must claim its share before the light can return.
outputs.L4:
**The Salt and the Silt**

The season turns upon a rusted hinge,
And shadow creeps into the cobblestone.
The twilight bleeds a faint and bruised fringe,
As winter claims the dark town for its own.
Through narrow lanes where bitter drafts collide,
A traveler treads the edge of sleep and space,
To watch the dying light of summer hide
Behind the blackened timber of the place.

Here, clocks have lost their hands to quiet rust,
Their brass gears choked on ash and frozen air;
The chiming bell-towers crumble into dust,
Unmarking hours no living soul can spare.
In shuttered rooms, the crooked dwellers wait,
Performing silent rites to summon sleep,
With faces carved of salt and hollow fate,
While slow decay begins its midnight creep.

Beside the river, thick with sunken ice,
A flooded graveyard whispers to the tide.
No holy verse, no silver sacrifice
Can keep the drowned beneath the mud inside.
And from the dark, a martyr starts to rise—
A spectral vision draped in river-weed,
With lilies fixed within her pale, blind eyes,
Submerged no more by mortal weight or deed.

Her translucent feet tread light upon the frost,
Her water-logged gown trailing like a shroud.
She bears the heavy reckoning of the lost,
Her quiet breathing cold against a cloud.
She haunts the crooked streets to testify
That flesh must turn to clay and bone to stone,
That every vibrant thing is born to die,
And drift into the dark, cold depths alone.

Yet in her rising from the river’s bed,
The cycle turns, unyielding and profound:
The seed lies buried underneath the dead,
Waiting for winter’s icy wheel to turn around.
For time is not a line, but shattered glass,
A recurring tide that washes clean the earth—
Where all we love and fear must surely pass,
Through decay, through cold, and into grim rebirth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, whimsical autumn poem in rhyming couplets about a surreal Halloween night, featuring weird folklore, trick-or-treating animals, and an eerie atmosphere.
counterfactuals.output:
The amber moon hung like a crooked coin,
Where severed shadows and the secrets join.
The pumpkin patches bled a violet frost,
And every path back home was swiftly lost.

The Spindle Witch began to weave the breeze,
To hang pale, hollow whispers from the trees.
A bone-flute piped beneath the barrow mound,
Where old, forgotten autumns stir the ground.

Out from the hedge the velvet badger stepped,
To knock on doors where stone gargoyles slept.
A dapper fox in tailored velvet gray,
Begged candied beetles for his night-time pay.

The marsh-hare skipped on feet of stitched-up lace,
A porcelain mask bound tight upon her face.
A parade of mice in shrouds of spider-thread
Sought yellow crumbs of butter from the dead.

Old Mrs. Moth passed out glass eyes and rust,
And plum-jam spiced with coffin-corner dust.
The crows carried pillowcases made of night,
To catch the drop of last year’s dying light.

The Jack-o’-Lanterns sneered with needle teeth,
And chewed the writhing shades that crept beneath.
A phantom boar emerged from blackest bogs,
To play a fiddle for the dancing frogs.

The church bell chimed a dark, thirteenth-hour tone,
And turned the woodland sweets to polished bone.
The masked beasts melted back into the fog,
And left the quiet world to dream of dark and bog.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a surreal ballad that mixes Halloween imagery, bizarre village characters (like an undertaker, a candy maker, and Baruch Spinoza), and a story about a drowned witch coming back to life.
counterfactuals.output:
The jack-o’-lanterns spat out moths,
The river turned to wine,
October draped the crooked roofs
In frost and spider-twine.
The moon was just a yellow tooth
Stuck in a throat of sky,
When Astrid rose from Black-Pond Depth
To watch the world go by.

Three hundred Halloweens ago,
They bound her to an oak,
And dragged her to the riverbed
Beneath a cloud of smoke.
They weighed her skirt with river-iron,
Her tongue with river-lead,
And swore no witch who drank the silt
Could ever leave the dead.

Now, Baruch Spinoza sat indoors,
A candle on his knee,
A-grinding glass for spectacle,
To make the blind man see.
"The water, witch, and wheel," he hummed,
"Are forged of self-same glue;
For God and Nature walk as one,
And so, sweet ghost, do you."

Outside, the undertaker worked—
Old Malachi the Grim—
He dug a grave straight up to heaven
On a ladder thin and slim.
He measured shadows with a thread
To catch a phantom’s waist,
And coffined up the autumn wind
With copper nails and haste.

Beside him stood the candy man,
Sir Thaddeus of the Sweet,
Who boiled a pot of beetle-wings
And glass to feed the street.
He candied all the village mice,
He glazed the dead men’s shoes,
And stirred a syrup made of teeth
And pale October bruised.

Then *GLUB* and *GURGLE* went the marsh!
The reeds caught violet fire,
The mud spat up a velvet shoe,
A length of rusted wire.
Out poked a hand of river-moss,
Out came a silver scream,
As Astrid climbed the lily-pads
And stepped out of the dream.

Her ribs were full of tadpoles,
Her dress was dripping gorse,
She rode upon the water-fog
As if it were a horse.
Her eyes were two black pebbles
Where the minnows used to spawn,
She breathed a breath of winter-cress
And walked upon the lawn.

"A box! A box!" the sexton cried,
"Her proportions are absurd!"
He tried to measure Astrid’s shade,
But only caught a bird.
The candy maker ran to her
With peppermint and gall:
"I’ll dip your rotted fingers, ma'am,
In sugar for the ball!"

He pushed a praline in her mouth,
She chewed it into glass;
She blew a kiss of water-weed
That turned his coat to grass.
The undertaker threw his shroud
To hide her naked bone,
She caught it in her slippery palms
And turned the cloth to stone.

Then down the lane to Baruch’s shop
The dripping lady stepped,
Where infinite geometry
And optical optics slept.
The philosopher looked up at her
Through polished, gleaming glass,
And did not flinch to see the sludge
Where living blood should pass.

"Good evening, Astrid," Baruch said,
"The Substance holds us all.
The wave that drowned you long ago
Is the wave that made you tall.
There is no sin, there is no hell,
No witch outside the mind—
You are the water, I the lens,
And God is merely blind."

She took the lens from Baruch’s hand
And pressed it to her throat;
It shone a beam of amber light
Across her mossy coat.
She saw the sky inside her chest,
She saw the stars above,
She saw the undertaker’s grave
Was filled with sugar-dove.

She laughed a laugh of bubbling silt,
She clapped her hands of clay,
And all the candied village mice
Began to sing and sway.
The jack-o’-lanterns closed their mouths,
The moon began to bleed,
As Astrid merged with stone and star,
With philosopher and weed.

Now every dreary Halloween,
When glass and iron rust,
Spinoza grinds the river-fog,
The baker candymakes the dust.
And deep within the muddy pond,
Where cold black waters run,
The drowned girl sits upon her throne,
At home with Everything and One.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming poem in the style of eerie magical realism focusing on the transition from autumn to winter, using uncanny motifs like a broken clock, humming pumpkins, and animals holding torches.
counterfactuals.output:
The iron sun began to sink,
The porch clock gave a shuddered chime,
Then stopped forever at the brink
Of some forgotten, secret time.
Its rusted hands refused to move,
Though autumn withered leaf by leaf;
It lodged within a frozen groove,
A silent monument to grief.

Out in the garden’s ruined bed,
The sunken gourds began to hum.
Not spoken words, but tones instead,
A drone that rendered crickets dumb.
They vibrated with hollow sound,
Their orange skins turned pale as bone,
And deep beneath the hardening ground,
The taproots echoed back the drone.

From tangled woods of ash and pine,
A quiet march came stepping slow:
The forest beasts in single line,
With torches lit in amber glow.
The badger bore a flickering branch,
The red fox held a rushlight high,
To guide the creeping avalanche
Of cold across the twilight sky.

They did not burn the sleeping grass;
Their fire cast a chilling gleam.
The pond was skinned in blackened glass,
Suspended in a breathless dream.
The flames burned blue, yet threw no heat,
Like ice caught in a pale delight,
As autumn laid its golden sheet
And slipped away into the night.

The humming gourds grew faint and small,
Their song locked underneath the ice.
The stillness swallowed one and all,
A landscape sculpted in a trice.
The beasts dissolved like rising smoke,
The broken clock remained unstrung,
And winter, soft and surreal, woke
To speak in an uncanny tongue.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a weirdly poetic AABB rhyming piece where a philosopher and a butcher dance like a two-headed beast, forest creatures beg at doors, and a moth flies out of a drowned martyr's mouth? Make it sound like an ancient dark folk tale.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath the black lake where the holy man lies,
The water-logged martyr with stones in his eyes,
Unclasps his cold jaw in the weed-tangled south,
And a pale velvet moth flutters out of his mouth.

It skitters away through the frost and the fog,
Past sleeping white foxes and rotted-out log,
To the edge of the woods where the creatures draw near,
To beg at the thresholds in sorrow and fear.

The stags with twined antlers and foxes with sores
Whine low for a crust at the heavy oak doors.
They knock with thin hooves on the iron and wood,
And pray for a crumb in the dark neighborhood.

While deep in the tavern, where tallow drips slow,
Two strange dancing shadows sway red in the glow.
A scholar of logic, a carver of swine,
Are stitched at the shoulder by cobweb and twine.

Together they reel like a two-headed beast,
To celebrate night at a shadow-bound feast.
One head speaks of cosmos, of virtue and mind,
While the other head grins with a cleaver behind.

The moth lands between them to finish the rhyme,
As meat meets the spirit and space meets with time.
And outside, the beasts beat their bones on the door,
While the two-headed monster glides over the floor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a spooky, atmospheric poem about fall.
counterfactuals.output:
The summer dies in quiet dread,
The maples weep in crimson red.
A bitter frost begins to creep,
To wake the things that should not sleep.

The sun becomes a pale, grey eye
That watches from a bruised-plum sky.
The garden rots, the sunflowers bend,
As light succumbs to Autumn’s end.

A heavy mist crawls from the wood,
Where ancient, knotty oak trees stood.
The dry leaves scrape across the street—
A sound like phantom, shuffling feet.

The howling wind begins to speak,
It makes the rusted iron squeak.
It blows out candles one by one,
And mocks the long-forgotten sun.

The veil grows thin, the lanterns glow,
While shadows stretch and secrets grow.
So pull your coat and lock the door,
The light won't save you anymore.

For October sits upon her throne,
And carves the world to dust and bone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
